question:
Patient note:
A 68-year-old woman is lying supine on a stretcher in the pre-operative holding bay awaiting an elective four-port laparoscopic sigmoid resection for symptomatic diverticulosis complicated by recurrent low-grade bleeding; the colorectal team anticipates 75–90 minutes of insufflation under general anesthesia with a planned two-night stay. She has been an inpatient on the medical ward for the past six days because each attempt to ambulate beyond the bathroom door provoked light-headedness and productive coughing fits related to a right lower-lobe consolidation that was identified on chest imaging nineteen days ago and treated with intravenous ceftriaxone followed by oral levofloxacin; during those six days nursing logs document fewer than 200 steps in total, and physical therapy notes indicate she has not yet progressed to corridor walking. The current nursing care plan designates her status as bed rest with bathroom privileges, so apart from assisted transfers she spends nearly the entire day in bed. Because repeated peripheral sticks failed during the pneumonia admission, a single-lumen peripherally inserted central catheter was placed in the left basilic vein on hospital day two; this morning the insertion site is clean beneath a transparent dressing, flushes effortlessly with saline, and withdraws brisk dark blood without pain, warmth, or drainage along the tract. The current hospitalization is otherwise uncomplicated; she has not visited an operating room, endoscopy suite, or interventional radiology lab in the past four weeks, and her last procedure—a remote open hysterectomy for benign disease—occurred more than two decades ago. Past medical records reveal a fifteen-year history of moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease attributed to 40 pack-years of cigarette exposure; she stopped smoking seven years ago and uses tiotropium daily with albuterol as needed, denies recent wheeze, but still becomes breathless climbing a single flight of stairs. She has never experienced orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, pedal edema, hospital admission for heart-failure decompensation, chest pressure suggestive of myocardial ischemia, cerebrovascular symptoms, intestinal inflammatory flares, or any malignant neoplasm. She reports no prior episodes of leg swelling, calf tenderness, unexplained shortness of breath, hemoptysis, or imaging-confirmed clots, and knows of no first-degree relatives who required anticoagulation for venous thrombosis. She has never worn a cast, utilized crutches, sustained fractures of the pelvis or long bones, or suffered multisystem trauma or spinal cord injury. Medications at bedside include tiotropium 18 µg inhaled once daily, albuterol 90 µg two puffs as needed, amlodipine 5 mg each morning for well-controlled hypertension, and a daily multivitamin; she is not receiving systemic corticosteroids, hormone therapy, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, antiplatelet drugs, or anticoagulants. Overnight vitals reveal temperature 36.6 °C, heart rate 82 beats min⁻¹ in regular rhythm, blood pressure 138/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 min⁻¹ with occasional raspy cough, and oxygen saturation 95 % on two liters nasal cannula; body mass index is 26 kg m⁻². She appears alert, converses in full sentences, and is oriented to person, place, and time. Airway assessment demonstrates Mallampati class II view, three-finger thyromental distance, intact dentition, and full neck extension. Jugular venous pulsation is not elevated; the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lung examination discloses diminished breath sounds with faint end-expiratory wheeze over both bases and scattered crackles over the right lower field that clear with coughing. The abdomen is soft with mild left lower-quadrant tenderness but no rebound or guarding; no hepatosplenomegaly is detected. Extremities are warm and well perfused, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+ bilaterally, calf circumferences measure 35 cm symmetrically, skin is free of varicosities, pigmentation, or pitting edema, and Homans sign is absent. Neurological screen shows 5/5 strength in all major muscle groups, intact sensation to light touch, and steady heel-to-shin once she sits at the edge of the bed, though she requests assistance to stand. Peripheral access consists of a 20-gauge catheter in the right forearm running lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate; sequential pneumatic compression sleeves are at the foot of the stretcher awaiting application after induction. Morning laboratory results drawn from the PICC: hemoglobin 12.4 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 37 %, platelets 232 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 8.1 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 137 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.0 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.92 mg dL⁻¹, AST 19 U L⁻¹, ALT 21 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.3 s with INR 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 28 s. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained yesterday shows interval improvement of the prior infiltrate, mild biapical emphysematous changes, and the catheter tip projecting at the cavo-atrial junction; a twelve-lead electrocardiogram printed this morning demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats min⁻¹ with preserved intervals and no acute ST-T changes. She has been nil per os since midnight, last albuterol was taken at 05:00, and the anesthesia team plans to administer pre-induction bronchodilator therapy while the colorectal service completes the surgical time-out.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The preoperative Caprini VTE score weights the following risk factors:
- Age 68 (61–74 years) → 2.
- BMI 26 kg/m² (>25) → 1.
- Planned laparoscopic resection lasting 75–90 minutes (>45 minutes) → 2. Count the operation once.
- Bed rest with bathroom privileges for six days (>72 hours) → 2.
- PICC with a central tip → 2.
- Pulmonary disease: pneumonia 19 days ago qualifies as recent serious lung disease. Counting pulmonary disease as one item gives 1 point; COPD is not added separately in this calculation.
Sum: 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 10. A Caprini form that lists recent pneumonia and chronic abnormal pulmonary function as separate qualifying items can give a different total.
Final answer: 10
